paragraphs.rawText: [IV.1.1] With Taricheae destroyed, the Romans held most of the cities and territories of Galilee, except that Gamala, a city in the region of Gaulanitis, sustained the spirit of a stubborn people, relying on its rugged position. For it stands on a mountain. Cut off on the right and left by sheer cliffs, it narrows towards the top; at the front it is severed by a deep chasm, while at the rear it spreads out somewhat. On that side too the approach is narrow and difficult, so that you would judge the road taken by those making for the city to resemble a tail. From its highest point it stretches out a neck to an immense distance, so that it presents its citadel like a head and raises it to a lofty height. Narrow at the beginning, with the ground, as it were, curving through winding slopes and sinking into the depths, it then raises a sort of tendon in the middle of its neck; the rest is steep and impassable. Hence many think that earlier generations called it Camela because it presents the form of a camel, but that the name Gamala became attached to the city through a corruption in the inhabitants’ usage. If you look at its closely joined buildings, you would judge it a city suspended in the air, and think especially that its northern parts hang down, while the southern parts bend back a little.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.1.2] Josephus had added fortifications to this city too. Relying on these and on the numbers of people flocking there, they had made a mockery of King Agrippa’s siege for seven months. For it, Sotanis and Seleucia were all parts of his kingdom. Seleucia lay beside that most pleasant grove of Daphne, renowned throughout Syria, interwoven with cypress trees and abounding in springs. Through these it pours nourishment, as from milky breasts, into the local river flowing past, which they call the Lesser Jordan. paragraphs.rawText: [IV.1.4] Agrippa, then, struck by a stone on his right elbow, withdrew from the fighting, and the Romans burst into the city. For the enemy yielded to missiles, the wall to rams. Those who had been obstructing the engines could no longer resist, and the wall, shaken by three rams, gave the besiegers an open route to the besieged. But impatience in their haste brought no slight disaster upon the victors. For when they poured into the houses, searching them or striving to seize the plunder first, the cramped dwellings gave way under the weight. Their foundations swayed and brought on a collapse, and each neighbouring building, crashing against the next, caused destruction. Many Romans, caught in these falls, met destruction in victory. Many, throwing themselves forward, were overwhelmed by fallen buildings; others were dragged out, their bodies mangled, scarcely half alive; dust killed many. Crowded into narrow spaces, they were cut down, while from above women, feeble old men and the younger men who had fled hurled stones upon those beneath them, or whatever kinds of missiles came to hand. Darkness had poured over everything, taken away sight and confounded the mind. In their ignorance they could find no way out.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.1.5] Thus, barely extricating themselves from danger, they left the city. Meanwhile Vespasian, pressing the enemy, had advanced into the interior of the city and kept the battle raging amid the hostile ranks surrounding him. For it did not befit so great a man to turn his back to the enemy, nor did he consider it safe. He had sent his son Titus to Syria. He roused his confidence in his well-known valour and gathered himself under arms. With shields locked together, he stood undaunted with the few men he had at hand, as though considering whom he should hurl himself upon. Dreading his onslaught, the Jews began to press him less vigorously, and each, fearing for himself, loosened the battle line. Thus Vespasian, facing the enemy, gradually drew back, more like a man fighting than one retreating. There fell Butius, a decurion, a man proven in many earlier wars and of known experience against the Jews and robust courage. A centurion too, with ten other Syrians, performed an outstanding and memorable deed. In the midst of the tumult, seeing the Romans hard pressed, he withdrew into the hidden parts of a house. There, while the Jews were talking over supper about what they had contrived against the Romans, he killed them all in the dead of night and presented himself again to the Roman army with his soldiers.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.2.1] When Vespasian saw that the army was dejected at the loss of so many men, and above all ashamed of having abandoned its commander, because they had left him alone inside the enemy’s city, he consoled them with the greatest goodwill, saying: “If the danger that fell to my lot causes you shame, I too had advanced to war to face dangers, not to avoid them. If, rather, it is because many of our men have been killed, there is nothing to wonder at: when is any victory won without bloodshed? Battles have their own outcomes. Although proven valour usually excels in war, something is commonly left to chance. But it belongs to the prudent man to correct a fall in adversity and to maintain moderation in prosperity. It belongs, on the contrary, to a rough and untrained mind always to presume upon success, as though the contest were not against men; it belongs to a weak man to lose confidence in the whole undertaking because of some fall, when all that happens in war may suddenly turn on the slightest impulses. Thus the best man is he who, sober amid adversity, wrestles with chance, trips up the stronger opponent and seeks to recover himself and correct his own falls. The less careful man, however, often falls through his own movements: rushing in heedlessly, he is thrown down by his own onslaught and lies prostrate. If this often happens where valour stands alone, how much more in war, where forces of different kinds meet in combat, with no single plan or shared judgement, where the ground is unfavourable and rugged, and the conditions of fighting in a confined space are unequal for many against few, since the very multitude is a burden to itself, while the few are less likely to miss among so many. But these things often steal upon us for a moment; they do not arise from valour, but happen by chance. There is therefore nothing that should distress you, fellow soldiers. It was not any weakness of your force, nor the courage of the Jews, that turned the course of events: the difficulty of the ground hindered our victory and gave them time to delay it. Nor is there anything to blame except an ill-considered and disorderly onslaught. For in following them to the higher parts of the city and rushing into their houses, you entangled yourselves in danger. You entered their dwellings; you took on their dangers. You held the city: who compelled you to go further inside? The enemy ought to have come down to you; you ought not to have striven recklessly for victory, forgetful of life and safety. Recover your spirits, then, and expect from your valour not merely consolation but, what is more, vengeance. You will certainly have me leading the way into battle. Be ready in spirit; may these dangers have made you stronger, not more timid. It is easy to redress an injury if valour recognises itself.”

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.3.1] With these words he kindled the soldiers’ courage. While they were repairing the rampart, many of the besieged slipped away from the siege by the steep places. For shortage of food was already assailing them, and they thought that the damaged stretches of wall would give way to the engines. Moreover, there was only one spring within the city, and that too was close to the walls. This put them in the greatest fear, so that very many slipped away. Those who thought they should remain, however, fought stubbornly.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.3.3] Yet the Romans refrained from entering the city when it lay open, until Titus returned and, stirred by distress at his father’s danger, burst into the city with a few men and inflicted very great slaughter upon the Jews. Those on the heights, however, rolled down stones and prevented the Romans from approaching; they hurled javelins and shot arrows. Stones pushed by the Jews rolled easily downhill, missiles reached their mark and arrows descended, not without danger to those they struck. For the Romans, hurling missiles towards the higher parts of the mountain was ineffectual, their effort fruitless and dangerous to themselves. Suddenly a storm of wind arose, turning back the Jews’ arrows and driving back their javelins, while carrying against the enemy whatever the Roman army hurled. Thus, overwhelmed by the barriers raised by the very elements and by whirling winds, all who were found there perished in the final destruction of the captured city. We have learnt, however, that four thousand were killed by the Romans and five thousand perished by falling from the heights; no age was spared.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.4.1] Gischala alone among the districts of Galilee had not yet drawn the enemy against itself, since the quieter dispositions of its inhabitants, a rural people content with their own produce, had no taste for war. But through the gathering of many men who made brigandage their way of life, even the inclinations of the milder people were corrupted by wicked habits. There was also a man named John, son of Levi, a native-born plague upon his people, second to none of the cunning in deceit, knowing no equal in wickedness. His desire to do harm had never failed him, though for a time poverty had prevented him from practising iniquity—yet I do not clearly know how to decide whether poverty had concealed him or restrained him. He was cunning in deceit, an artist in deception, skilled at winning belief through lies and securing credulity through fabrications. He regarded deceit as a virtue and thought it a mark of refinement to cheat those dearest to him. He was ready to conspire, vehement in daring, keen in carrying things out; a troublemaker in times of quiet, a deserter in danger; accustomed to brigandage, inexperienced in war. Though he could not conduct wars, he nevertheless sowed them to prepare the way for his own rule. His mind, then, was restless, his audacity ready and nourished by successes, and he had wealth with which to gather a band of reprobates.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.4.2] When Vespasian learnt that the people of the aforesaid city were being roused to war by John’s faction, he sent his son Titus with a thousand horsemen, so as not to weary the entire army. Accompanied by them, Titus approached the city. But when he saw the walls crowded with people, he said that he was amazed that they followed in rebellion the example of those whose destruction ought to have brought them to their senses. “Granted, however, that their first attempts offered some ground for confidence, what hope could the destruction of them all hold out? Their hopes of freedom may certainly have been pardonable at the beginning, but perseverance when all is lost and beyond hope is unforgivable. For against those who are moved neither by an example of humanity nor by earnest verbal admonition, words are not needed, but arms. You trust in walls, as though they had protected anyone against Roman valour. What else can men shut in display, men besieged put forward, except their boldness in captivity?”

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.4.3] No one had the freedom to speak; the band of brigands had occupied the entire circuit of the walls. John was taking care that no one should invite the Romans in through friendly conversation. He therefore forestalled any reply, saying that he willingly accepted discussion of their common affairs and did not refuse to try it: he himself might perhaps offer useful advice, or have to assent to what was proposed. But he was forbidden by ancestral law to discuss conditions of peace, since the day of the sacred week had not yet passed. Just as taking up arms was forbidden, so it was also unlawful to deliberate on peace on holy days. For to decide on business even in words was sacrilege for those compelled to do so, and would not go unpunished for those who compelled them. He asked the indulgence of a single day; so small a delay would be no hindrance. For, with the enemy surrounding them, those shut in had no free means of escape. Was he being offered a choice of peace? With so fair a choice, there was no fear. Meanwhile he ought not to be pressed into deliberations on peace, when he and his people held it a religious scruple to transgress their ancestral law. Moreover, it was fitting, with so generous an offer of peace, that the man who freely offered peace beyond expectation, so that no one should face danger, should also preserve their own laws for those who would escape it. Titus thought these arguments had been put forward without deceit, sounded the retreat and recalled from the walls those he had brought with him.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.4.4] Thus John obtained the opportunity to flee and departed in the dead of night with many others. Women too followed him as he went. But the further the men advanced, the more women and little children were left behind. Abandoned by their own people, the frightened women watched the road. When their husbands were already passing out of sight, they thought the enemy was at hand and trembled at every sound. If anyone ran, the wretched women turned round, afraid that they were being attacked and chains were being put upon them, as though those they feared were already present.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.4.5] In accordance with the agreement, Titus made for the city with his army once the sun had shed its light. The gates were opened; the people came out in exultation and welcomed the Romans with joy and eagerness, glad that the pestilent man had gone. He had fled during the night, they said, and they had been given the freedom to decide for themselves. They begged pardon, asking that the flight of a man whom they could not have held without their own destruction should not count against them. Consoling himself for the postponement of vengeance with the speed at which the business had been completed, Titus immediately sent many men to seize John, in case they might catch up with him. He himself entered the city and, content to have dealt with the disturbers of peace by threats rather than punishment, pardoned everyone. He did so lest anyone, stirred by hatred or private disputes, should bring odium upon innocent men and assail them with a charge of the gravest crime, since it is far more tolerable to leave an uncertain matter to the fear of a complicit conscience than to condemn an innocent man. For fear often corrects a guilty man, but there is no remedy for the punishment of an innocent man. Those whom Titus had sent did not find John, but they did find the little children and women who were following him. About two thousand were killed; three thousand of vulnerable age and sex were assigned to captivity once the appetite for killing had been sated. He gave the city a military garrison. Thus all Galilee was brought under Roman power.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.5.1] Thus far we may be allowed our digression, as we have kept our pen occupied with other cities, shrinking from the defilements of the holy temple founded by our ancestors and of the sacred law. But now it is time to undertake the account of what happened at Jerusalem, not trusting in our ability, but lest we seem to have denied our ancestral law and ancient worship the service of our grief. Though there may have been in them shadow, not truth, yet shadow marks the traces of truth. For a shadow has the outlines of a picture, but lacks its brilliance; it has not received the finishing touch, yet to those who look closely it portrays what is to come. Thus the figure gives less delight; grace attracts more. Hence it pleased the arbiter of all things to abolish the old and establish the new, so that those who, through the narrowness of faithlessness, did not follow the images might follow the truth.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.6.1] Fleeing from the regions of Galilee, as we said above, John made his way to the city of Jerusalem and, like a kind of plague, infected the minds of many who, foremost in outrage, had flowed there from various regions as into a cesspool. For this was a cause of greater destruction for that city: the service the reprobates rendered to their crimes—many gathering there where they believed they would either be safer or more unrestrained in heaping up their outrages—was thought to be service rendered to faith. They were therefore received everywhere as though they had come to defend the temple out of devoted love for it. This was the first blight of these evils.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.6.2] Hence the gentleness of the few was overwhelmed by the insolence of the many. Hence they proceeded to killings, since an outsider was less inclined to spare anyone. Hence they conspired to neglect the observances of the law and transfer priesthoods from good men to wicked ones, because men who were strangers not only to devoted worship but to the very knowledge of the law did not know what was holy. First, men of royal stock who resisted were bound, so that the rest would yield through fear; then they were killed. To conceal the outrage, they falsely claimed that the men whom they had killed without trial by sending assassins into the prison had been put to death on a fabricated charge of treason. Fear therefore struck them all. Since powerful and innocent men—Antipas, Levias and Foras—had been so easily overwhelmed, they no longer dared to resist.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.6.3] From this they went so far as to install obscure and unworthy men as chief priests. Men whom no claim of merit commended for the honour obtained priesthoods contrary to their deserts and were made subject, in every wicked deed, to the will of those who bestowed them.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.6.4] But when the men of the priesthood opposed them, and above all Ananus, senior to the others, the rebels called for the chief priest to be chosen by lot, so that the prerogative of the highest title should not be bestowed through favour. In this way the outcome of the lot would be regarded as entrusted not to favour but to divine judgement. They did indeed invoke an ancient custom, by which those to be appointed to the chief priesthood were ordinarily summoned to the lot; in fact, however, they were plainly working to dissolve the law.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.6.5] For the law selected for the lot men of priestly succession, but they, for appearances, brought forward a single one of the priestly tribes, named Eniachim, and ordered the choice to be made by lot. Then a certain Phanis, son of Samuel, a villager, was chosen by the lot. He not only lacked any succession traced through the chief priests, but had no knowledge at all of priestly office, since he occupied himself in the country and therefore did not know what a chief priest was. In short, he was dragged unwillingly from the fields and made to assume another’s role, as though on a stage. He was also clothed in the vestments consecrated by ancient custom and taught on the spot what he ought to do. Thus the outcome of the lot exposed the wickedness of the seditious men, when the exercise of so great a priesthood was handed down to an ignorant rustic. But the evasion of the ancient observance was a jest to them and a grief to the priests, who wept and groaned that the law was being mocked by reprobates.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.6.6] Yet, relying on the authority of devotion itself and on the indignation of good men, they gathered together and rushed upon the disturbers.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.6.7] But the others, distrusting both their cause and their numbers, fled to the temple as to a citadel and established it as a kind of camp from which to repel the crowd of people rushing upon them. At first they stood before the temple doors and in its very vestibule, fighting against the people. Anyone who had been wounded made for the interior of the temple, pouring his blood upon the inner threshold and wiping his bloodied face upon the pavements. Wounds and the flesh of open wounds were packed with garments they were not permitted to touch. There was war within the city, war among citizens, war before the temple. The brigands showed no reverence even for this: when the people pressed them more fiercely, they withdrew inside the temple itself and immediately closed the doors. This barrier checked Ananus, lest he seem to be bringing war upon the temple and breaking through the temple doors consecrated by ancestral religious observance. He turned back the people’s onslaught and stationed six thousand men in the porticoes, armed to stand guard and keep a vigilant watch. Gradually, however, he softened his resolve and sought peace, chiefly from his concern that the blood of citizens should not defile the temple. He urged that an embassy be sent to mediate peace, so that civil war might be laid aside.

An oath was demanded; he did not refuse, lest by refusing he should lose the benefit of perjury. He pretended to favour the people in order to deceive them.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.6.11] Thus they were won over and came without delay. Twenty thousand men assembled, intent on no cultivation of the land but ready for brigandage.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.6.12] The arrival of the Idumaeans could not escape Ananus’s notice. He ordered the gates to be closed, so that they should not enter in tumult but, if possible, learn the truth and renounce war.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.7.1] The chief priests therefore climbed the wall and addressed the Idumaeans from a tower. They were utterly amazed, they said, that, so swiftly ensnared by lies, the Idumaeans were pursuing by arms causes they had not yet understood. They ought to have been judges of disputes before becoming fighters in wars, and above all to have learnt the merits of the case before taking up arms—arms against men of their own stock, their own worship, their own observance. No greater injury had been inflicted upon anyone than upon the Idumaeans, who were being stirred to share in such grave outrages. For what else was being asked of them but the murder of their own kin—their fellow citizens—and sacrilege against the temple? Different aims and different characters did not ordinarily agree with one another. Similarity of character creates fellowship in purpose and binds kindred aims together. The most wicked men, who maintained their livelihood by brigandage, had presumed to summon the Idumaeans as allies, although the Idumaeans’ purpose differed so greatly from that of those who had called them: “Those men have brought war upon their own country, yet have entreated you to come as though to defend a city not your own. You, who are innocent, have nothing in common with plunderers; you, who are sober, have nothing in common with men who make themselves drunk. If only that drunkenness were of wine and not of fury! Once they have gorged themselves on outrages, squandering their own inheritances, they plunder the property of others; and what they have wickedly gained they squander still more wickedly and pour away still worse. There is no end to their plundering, because there is no limit to their gluttonous consumption. When they have drenched themselves in wine and filled themselves with drunkenness, they belch out a surfeit of public affairs, so that they may become drunk again on our blood and mock holy religion, which has always been an object of veneration and reverence to you. Flee, then, these gatherings for the murder of kin, abandon their sacrilegious ventures, forsake the assemblies of brigands. You have been called to a share in crime: let your coming bring a remedy to your country. We see a most distinguished people, who ought to have come at the request of a public council, to give aid against the enemy to the most eminent city of the Jews, held to be the mother-city of the whole nation. But even if we failed to ask, while hoping for peace and unwilling to weary you hastily—we were offering peace to the stirrers of war—nevertheless, as though you had come by divine judgement, deliberate for the common good and present yourselves as arbiters between both sides. Ask where the disturbance began; who sounded the war trumpet in a peaceful city; who shed the blood of its most eminent citizens; at whose instigation punishment was exacted from men not condemned; who brought destruction upon us before the Romans did. We were preparing war against the Romans, yet were already suffering these men as enemies. Whose favour with the Romans, then, is suspect: that of the men who avenge the Romans, or that of the men who repel them? These things are certainly more grievous to us than battles with the Romans. At their hands we would die for freedom; by these men we are butchered as though for a crime. Charges of treason are invented against the innocent, and the accusation is fabricated after death, although investigation ordinarily precedes punishment, not punishment investigation. For what does it profit a dead man to be acquitted, when he is no longer answerable to judgement? Yet we accept even a fate of this kind, that our innocence should be investigated after our killing; and we willingly plead before you too the case for our own integrity and that of the dead, although you stand armed on behalf of our adversaries. So utterly do our accusers lack arguments that their case is the worse even before you, who believed them so quickly. For a good judge grieves at having been deceived by lies and is therefore more hostile to the deceiver than to the man attacked, because he thinks he must take vengeance for having been rashly induced to believe falsehoods. Preserve, then, an impartial examination for us, and gather the truth from the course of events, not from the weaving of words. First of all, why should we betray our country to the Romans, whom we could have refrained from provoking? Perhaps that was what we ought to have done, so as not to rouse the conquerors of all nations. But deliberation on this is no longer part of our present task. It belonged to an earlier time to choose what course we should follow; now we must fall for freedom. For it is better to die for one’s country. It might have been more advantageous before the war to prefer peace to death; but since war is at our necks, many of our brothers have already been captured, others killed, and there is grief for the dead and groaning for those in chains, a free death must be chosen rather than a life of captivity. Yet it remains open to those about to die to wipe away the disgrace of the false charge of treason. Before you, Idumaeans, we plead our case: let those privy to it, the intermediaries who conveyed the messages, be exposed and brought forward. If they have informers, let them produce them; if they have none, why do they accuse us and charge us on empty suspicions they have themselves devised? They ought not to allege what they cannot prove. But because they do not dare to accuse us openly, they wish to spread it among the crowd, and therefore rush into war to avoid being called to judgement. For in war there is a chorus of fury; in peace, an examination of truth. See, we are here first; we offer ourselves willingly for punishment, if only an accuser comes forward. Or if odium is being turned upon the people, inquire more carefully what the purpose of the public assembly was. Was it not to prepare forces equipped for war, so that each man should help his country in the cause of freedom? Against the brigands themselves, what had been resolved except that peace should be agreed? The grief of individuals, the blood of the innocent, the groaning of women and the violation of ancestral statutes had sharpened public indignation. The groaning of all rang out, because each feared the same things for himself. Priesthoods were being bestowed upon the most unworthy men. They began to be attacked with cries; they struck down the people with stones and killed them with weapons. Public grief blazed up; they established refuges for brigands in the temple. Thus the place of peace, revered even by the nations, and the dwelling of holiness became an assembly-place of plunderers. Where people used to flock from every part of the earth to worship at the festal celebration, there are now dens of wild beasts wet with human blood. You may investigate these things even while armed, but without the law of war. Judgement has often taken place amid arms, and justice has laid aside the instruments of war; the verdict of equity has silenced the trumpets. You can turn to the defence of the city these arms which you took up for its overthrow. You may also enter unarmed, hear everything and inquire into it. If you find any slackness towards the enemy, deem it treason. But if you wish to act neither as our defenders nor as arbiters, why are you surprised that the gates are not opened to armed men? They are closed against arms, not against kinsmen. Lay aside war, and the gates will open.”

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.8.1] When the priests had spoken in this way, especially Jesus, who was senior to the others but came after Ananus and held second place, the Idumaeans were indignant that they had not immediately been received into the city. Simon, one of the Idumaean commanders, said: “It is no wonder that they rage against their fellow citizens and keep them shut in, when they have closed the gates against an allied nation and do not allow their fellows and partners to enter. They speak to us from the wall and repel us with walls as though we were adversaries, when they had us as friends. Who can doubt that they are preparing to receive the Romans and perhaps to crown the gates when they enter? What greater injury could there be? This city is accustomed to lie open to all men for religious observance; to us alone it is barred, as though we were enemies. We alone are disowned, we alone are repelled. They pretend to seek our judgement, though they did not think us worthy even of the city’s threshold. Let what they have done against those men remain hidden: we are witnesses and judges of our own injury. We see what those shut in suffer, when we ourselves are ordered to lay down our arms. Can it be believed that they await the judgement of men whose faithfulness they suspect? Let us hasten, then, to rescue those shut in, for whom the temple has become a prison, lest they be kept until the arrival of the Roman army and handed over as captives to Vespasian. Let us lift the siege from the temple and remove the foulest of guards, who allow no one to go out even to empty his bowels. If anyone wishes to bring food to those shut in, he is prevented; if anyone wishes to go out, he is dragged to death. Religious worship has been made a crime.”

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.9.1] On hearing this, Jesus withdrew, considering it vain to struggle against God’s adverse will, since hostile uproar resounded both within and without, and the city was being assailed from both sides. The Idumaeans raged at being excluded; those stationed in the temple contrived how to join them. Fear troubled the latter, lest the Idumaeans should leave before accomplishing their purpose, while shame deprived the others of the will to return. Distrust had already almost crept over them when suddenly, in the night, an unbearable gale arose, a black storm. The winds roared, the sky grew terrible, torrents of rain poured down; there were dreadful flashes of lightning, monstrous peals of thunder and a bellowing of the earth, so that the world seemed to be dissolving. paragraphs.rawText: [IV.9.2] The people’s judgement, however, was uncertain and divided. Some thought that the supreme God, indignant at the Idumaeans because they had come armed against their fellows, had stirred up the storms. Ananus and the more penetrating minds among the elders conjectured that the harm suffered by the Idumaeans was rousing them still more to destroy their allies. Ananus, more watchful on other nights, that night was undone, not by bodily weariness but rather by despair of spirit. He yielded to events flowing against him and to the storms of the world fighting for his destruction. paragraphs.rawText: [IV.9.3] Then they came to the wall and opened the gate near the assembled Idumaeans. That would have been the last day of the whole people, had the Idumaeans not thought they should make for the temple before entering the heart of the city. paragraphs.rawText: [IV.9.4] When this had succeeded as intended, they all poured out together from the temple as though from a camp, their battle line extended, and slaughtered throughout the streets whomever they found, some asleep, others terrified. Prayers availed nothing, tears nothing, marks of honour nothing; no services won favour. All were indiscriminately butchered. Seeing the bestial savagery of their pursuers, and that no one was spared, they hanged themselves: an end more pitiable, as it seems to me, than being killed by the enemy, because voluntary death is ascribed to savagery, and the hideous knot of the noose is reckoned a disgrace as well. But what room was there for counsel, where the fear of punishment was so great, when each man feared not death but the torments before death, for which death would be a remedy? Blood overflowed everywhere, and especially around the temple, because those guarding the men shut in had gathered there. That day eight thousand five hundred slain men were found.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.10.1] There was in the city a man named Zacharias, who hated the wicked and did not mingle with evildoers. He was rich in wealth, whose abundance they thought could either be effective in breaking up their faction or offer them rich plunder. They decided to summon him on a charge of treason. But he, with a conscience clear of any such thing, began to speak freely in his own defence, not only refuting the charges but also establishing that they themselves were guilty of the gravest outrages. The case was heard before seventy men. All acquitted him, because nothing connected with a crime was brought forward. But the others rushed upon him and hurled him into the depths. They drove out the judges, not only insulting them but also putting them in danger, so that their example would warn the rest against presuming in future to show firmness in judgement contrary to their will.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.10.2] Again, however, so that no one should be acquitted, they themselves became the executors of their anger and killed whomever they pleased without trial. Gorgon, a pleasing and lovable man, was slain. So too was Niger the Peraean, who had been chosen among Judaea’s defenders to safeguard its highest interests. A warrior, who even bore the marks of his valour in the scars of his wounds, he was dragged to death. When he saw that he was being led outside the city, he began to beg, no longer for life, but for burial. Yet not even to this pitiable petition did he receive an answer consistent with mercy. False charges were fabricated: if anyone bought himself free, he was innocent; the man who offered no money was struck down as guilty.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.11.1] While these things were happening at Jerusalem, Vespasian meanwhile was subduing other parts of the Jewish nation. News reached him of the strife at Jerusalem, the deaths they had inflicted upon themselves in domestic battles, and the punishments citizens had exacted from citizens. Many urged him to proceed there, lest anything be taken away from Rome’s triumph and his own glory. But he was a moderate and far-sighted man, who judged advantageous not what accorded with common practice, but what, on deeper consideration, he thought would benefit the whole undertaking. He began to reply to those giving this advice that the state was not always helped by battles, but often glory was won and the debt to the fatherland paid even by laying down arms. “What difference does it make how the enemy is defeated, by our sword or his own, except that by his own he is overthrown without odium attaching to Rome? For they cannot complain of us when they have wounded one another. At the same time they show how justly they have made war upon us, since they do not spare even themselves. This would seem vengeance from heaven, that those who have provoked the Romans should rage in madness. But if anyone asserts that something is being taken from our glory, let him recognise that a remedy achieved in silence always outweighs a battle fought with danger. Indeed, our Maximus broke Hannibal more by delaying than by fighting. Although the Scipios subdued Africa, victory in war is shared with many; to Maximus alone was it granted to restore the Roman state by delaying. It is therefore a greater thing to have preserved the Roman dominion than to have extended it. Yet let us reckon the merits of these valiant deeds equal. Surely, in war itself, the devices of wisdom are no less than the distinctions of courage. Let them therefore perish by their own arms: nothing is taken from our praise, and a very great deal is added to our victory. Those whom we spare do not know how to preserve their own people. What if, when we begin to threaten them, they perhaps come to their senses and are reconciled with one another? I do not fear this, but put it forward against your view. Or, if the strife persists, should it appear that they have defeated themselves, that the Roman army has done nothing, that our hands have been idle, and that victory has been won not by our valour but by the enemies’ mutual slaughter? The wiser course, then, is for them to rage to their own destruction in our absence, lest anyone think that they have been harassed more by our intrigues than by their own. We shall do better to approach when a victor remains to be added to our triumph. Certainly, let those who flee their own people come to us; let those whom the scourge of their own people has driven out find safety with us.”

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.12.1] Vespasian’s expectation did not deceive him. For those who could buy their release fled to the Romans. Every paved road and every path was filled with fugitives. The rich were let go; the poor, who lacked money for their ransom, were killed. Many also greatly feared ambushes and brigandage outside the city, especially the poor, who had no escort. Thus they faced equal danger outside and at home, deadly in either case; yet to many, in the hope of burial in their native land, death among their own people seemed more tolerable.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.13.1] When fear, spread among all by the immense slaughter of the people, had made everyone subject to the faction, John, not content to exercise power in common with the leaders of the faction, began to aspire to tyranny and resented an equal. He therefore overturned the decrees of others, recognised nothing as valid except what pleased him, and gradually attached bodyguards to himself. Skilled in deceit, he ensnared by fraud those he wished, bound them to himself with money, and terrified them with power; by these arts he had joined very many to himself. Yet there were also men who rejected servitude, even at peril to themselves, especially since, accustomed to rule, they could not endure slavery. Thus three kinds of deadly calamity contended in one city: tyranny, war and strife, each of which could destroy not one city but many. Yet of the three, war was the lighter evil, and an enemy in regular warfare seemed more tolerable than a tyrant or a faction.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.13.2] To these was added a fourth kind, that of the Sicarii. Seeing the city occupied by the upheavals of tyranny or the tumults of strife, they ravaged all the neighbouring places and carried everything away. They put to death women and children who, through the weakness of their sex or age, could not endure the hardship of the journey. Seven hundred in number were thus killed. Grain was conveyed into the strongholds. They rushed upon fields, cities and temples, carried off plunder, and let no opportunity for killing pass. In the guise of an army they practised brigandage, in greater numbers than the practice of brigandage required. They made war more bitter with the savagery of brigandage, allowing no pardon for surrender or mercy in receiving those who submitted.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.14.1] Thus Vespasian, from whom destruction had been feared, was asked to come as a remedy. He hastened to Gadara, where there were very many wealthy men who, on account of their estates, were increasingly afraid of the brigands’ ambushes and raids. They had therefore secretly sent to Vespasian to ask him to approach them, so that the city might be rescued from the brigands. The Roman army arrived. On seeing it, the Gadarenes wished to flee to it, but could find no way to do so without destruction to themselves, lest the faction rise against them as they departed and destroy them all. Yet it did not escape the faction that Vespasian had been invited by an embassy of the Gadarenes and that Dolesus, a leading man of the city, was privy to that embassy. The faction seized and killed him; having avenged the affront, they left the city and withdrew to hidden and more strongly fortified places. Gadara was handed over to the Romans, and Vespasian was received with great applause. He at once sent Placidus to pursue those who had fled, and himself returned to Caesarea.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.15.1] Placidus sent five hundred horsemen ahead and pursued the fugitives, forcing them into the nearest village. Finding there a picked body of young men, they took courage to rise against the Romans. This brought them very great disaster. For the cavalry surrounded them and cut them off from the village, and they were killed without any hindrance; while others withdrew in a mass, they were slaughtered before the thresholds of the gates. A mound heaped up from the bodies of the slain had reached the height of the walls.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.15.2] The Romans pierced some with arrows and wounded others with various missiles; at last they stormed the stronghold, and all within were killed except those who had the opportunity to escape. Others, as they fled, magnified by their words the great fame of Roman valour: the bodies they had seen were larger than human bodies, and no one had any confidence of resisting the unconquered. Hence all were terrified and fled at once. Not only neighbouring and adjoining places were abandoned, but even the city of Jericho, which, because of the throngs of its inhabitants, had sustained the hopes of the rest. With events going as he wished, Placidus pursued these too with his horsemen, striking down some in masses and others as they strayed, as far as the river Jordan. At the riverbank too he found a very great number whose passage was blocked, because the aforesaid river happened then to have swollen with rain or melting snow. When they saw the Romans at hand, they made ready and crowded along the edge of the river. With the refuge of flight cut off, necessity put the remedy into their hands, and the many charged and hurled themselves upon the fewer horsemen. These, with familiar skill and in the old manner of soldiering, began to ride between them, break up the enemy’s wedge, disperse their masses, press the weary and pursue those who yielded. Thus some were killed by the enemy’s weapons, others by their own, upon which they fell as they were crowded together and dashed against one another. Others rushed into the river, where their very fall and their entanglement with one another submerged them. Many also entrusted themselves to the river, thinking they could cross it; when they had advanced a little, the force of the eddies swallowed them or the rush of the river swept them away. Even those who, practised in swimming, had made progress over the water and kept themselves afloat above the current flowing beneath, lost their lives in the river, caught in the branches of trees carried down by it or crushed by the trunks themselves. Often too a man unskilled in swimming, on grasping a swimmer, held fast so that he too might escape, and wore him out, locked in his arms, until both sank, each bringing destruction upon the other. And if someone, carried down by a favourable current, seemed likely to escape, he was sewn through with arrows and suddenly perished face upwards, the oars of his arms ceasing to move. There were also men who, unable to swim and seeking a painless death, flung themselves willingly from a raised bank into the river; others entered from a sandy shore, their feet sank, and they were drawn down. Many too slipped on rounded stones or stumbled in the shallows, swayed with unsteady footing and were overwhelmed by the currents following them. Thirteen thousand were killed by the sword, while an innumerable multitude was consumed by the river. Immense plunder was gained from flocks of sheep and herds of camels, asses and cattle.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.15.3] Although this slaughter of men was very great, it was nevertheless reckoned greater than it really was. For not only was the whole region filled with human bodies, since the scattered and straying were killed wherever they were caught, but the Jordan itself was so obstructed by the bodies of the dead that it could not maintain its own course. Lake Asphaltites too, into which everything the Jordan had drawn along was carried, changed its natural appearance through the blood and entrails of the dead. Indeed, it was reckoned that ninety-two thousand two hundred Jews had perished that day at the hands of only five hundred horsemen and three thousand foot soldiers. Advancing further, Placidus also restored Abila, Julias, Bethesmon and all the villages of that district as far as Lake Asphaltites to the Roman dominion. He also put soldiers into boats to kill all who had fled into the aforesaid lake.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.16.1] Thus these places too, and everything as far as Machaerus, were recovered. Vespasian, however, was awaiting the time for battle, when he would attack the chief city of all Judaea with the Roman army. Meanwhile, as he was occupied with the affairs entrusted to him, news reached him of fresh disturbances in the regions of Gaul: certain powerful men of the Roman army had deserted Nero. On learning this, he wished to bring the turmoil of wars in the East to an end and bring relief from the civil wars and the danger to the whole state and the entire Roman dominion, so as either to suppress or forestall all disturbances in Italy with news of successes. As soon as the rigours of winter had been tempered by the beginning of spring, he set out from Caesarea with the greater part of the army. The city called Antipatris received him. Advancing from there, he burned villages and killed those he found hostile; above all, he ravaged whatever places he encountered near the Idumaeans, because they were a restless race of men, friendly to wars rather than leisure or quiet. He also seized two villages of Idumaea, Legaris and Caphartor, and shattered their inhabitants by immense slaughter. More than ten thousand men were killed; he carried off a thousand captives and drove out the rest of the populace, to station a force of his own men there, since the mountainous places of that region were infested with brigandage. He himself returned with the army to Amathus, which took its name from hot waters, since the vapour of water is said to be called amathus in the language of Syria. paragraphs.runningText: Thus these places too, and everything as far as Machaerus, were recovered. paragraphs.rawText: [IV.16.2] At the news of the Roman army’s approach, many had left the city of Jericho for the mountains of the region of Jerusalem, since they saw that it was unsafe. The whole multitude of those who remained was destroyed. For it was not difficult to capture the city quickly: it was supported by no natural defence and had been deserted and abandoned by its own people as they slipped away. The city is built on a plain, above which rises a broad mountain bare of vegetation. For it extends northwards as far as the territory of the city of Scythopolis, while to the south it stretches as far as the region of Sodom and the boundaries of Asphaltites. The soil is poor and barren, and therefore deserted by inhabitants, since its natural sterility makes it of no use to cultivators. Opposite it is a mountain beyond the Jordan, which begins to rise from Julias and the northern quarter. It extends southwards as far as Sobaros in Arabia, bordering on Petra, where there is also a mountain called Iron by ancient usage. Between these two mountains lies a plain which the inhabitants, by ancient usage, have called Great because of its size, since it extends over a vast space. Its length is two hundred and thirty stades, its breadth a hundred and twenty; it begins at the village of Genuabari and ends at Lake Asphaltites. The Jordan cuts through the middle of this plain, not merely leaving its beauty unimpaired but adding to it: the banks grow green through the river’s flooding, and the lakes Asphaltites and Tiberias follow in succession, sharing one source but differing in character. For the water of the one tastes salt and is barren in its use, while that of Tiberias is sweet and life-giving. In the days of summer, however, excessive heat burns over the expanse of the plain. Hence, as the blight of excessive drought combines with the dryness of the ground, the air grows more corrupt and causes pitiable illnesses among the inhabitants. For everything is dry except the edge of the river. Indeed, in the more distant places even the fruit of trees grows sickly, since the yield of palms growing on the banks of the river Jordan is both more abundant and richer, while elsewhere it is far poorer.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.17.1] There is also beside the city of Jericho an abundant spring, rich in water for drinking and nourishing for irrigation, which Joshua son of Nun, a Hebrew by nation and mighty in hand, first wrested from the nation of the Canaanites. At first it was considered corrupt, barren in generation and of little wholesome use to those who drank it. Hence the prophet Elisha, Elijah’s disciple and a successor by no means unworthy of so great a master, was asked by the inhabitants of the places he had visited to leave them a reward for their hospitality and relieve the corruption of the waters. He gave a remedy, as the ancient Scripture of Kings teaches, ordering an earthen vessel with salt to be brought to him. Taking it, he threw the salt into the spring and said: “I have healed these waters, and no one will die in them or be made barren by them.” “And the waters were healed,” it says, “according to the word of the prophet Elisha.” From that time, then, the waters were tempered by the infusion of blessed salt, the mouth of the spring was opened, and the courses of its waters were sanctified, so that the gushing of its veins poured forth sweeter draughts and all that bitterness of the waters grew sweet. The earth gave richer fruits, and a fruitful succession of children born supplied an abundance of posterity. Nor did the life-giving water fail, upon which divine grace had breathed through the blessings of so great a prophet, in response to the faithful zeal of the righteous. Thus, at the prophet’s prayers, the answering voice of the heavenly oracle changed the nature of the waters and at once drove out sterility and poured in fertility. Generations of men and the fruits of the earth began to multiply there. The water, formerly barren and bitter, accustomed to kill the crops and twist the mouths of drinkers with its harshness, began to pour fertility into the soil and sweetness into those who drank, so that, if it touched cultivated ground there only briefly, it did more good than where it had watered for longer. For this is a new grace: the increase is more abundant where the use is less, and where anyone has used more, the yield is less. It therefore irrigates more than other springs, because even a little of it is more than enough for fertility. Indeed, a plain surrounds it, extending seventy stades in length and twenty in breadth. In it you may see the wonderful grace of gardens, various kinds of palms, and dates of such sweetness that you may watch honey flowing from them, by no means inferior to other honey. There are also excellent broods of bees there; nor is this surprising, where gardens breathe upon such varied flowers and pour forth sweet scents. Opobalsam is produced there. We use the name with this addition because farmers cut through the bark of the twigs in which balsam is produced, so that the liquid dripping gradually through those openings may collect. An opening is called opē in Greek. They report that henna grows there, and myrobalan, and other things of this kind that are nowhere found in other places. The water is like other spring water. Yet here it is superior: cold in summer, warm in winter; the air is milder, so that in the depth of winter the inhabitants wear linen clothing.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.18.1] Let us now consider the character of Lake Asphaltites. For it is better to occupy the pen with descriptions of ancient places or the marvel of the other elements than with the strife of the Jews, since the latter exasperates the mind by its wickedness, while the former soothe the spirit as they are recounted and recall it to knowledge of ancient history. But we, whose talent is uncultivated, are eager to retrace the footsteps of the fathers as they went out of Egypt as far as the land of resurrection, so that, if our writings should happen to come into anyone’s hands, he may read not our words but reread those of the fathers. For it is sweeter to dwell among the habitations of our ancestors, recall to memory the words and deeds of the ancients, and cling to their grace. But now let us describe the nature or character of the waters, lest our pen too be cast out of that lake, from which, it is believed, all living things you might think could be submerged nevertheless rebound and, however violently dashed into it, are at once cast out. The water itself is bitter and barren, admitting no kind of living creature. Indeed, it tolerates neither fish nor birds accustomed to water and delighting in diving. They say that a lighted lamp floats upon it and, without being overturned, sinks when its light is extinguished, and that whatever is alive, submerged by any contrivance, can scarcely remain in the depths. Indeed, they say that Vespasian ordered men who could not swim to be thrown into the depths with their hands bound, and that all at once floated, as though lifted by a breath of wind, and sprang back, driven upwards with great force. Many have thought much of what is told of this lake fabulous; as we have not tested these things, we have had no intention of declaring the truth of the matter. Nor have we chosen to set down as true that the water changes colour three times a day and gleams variously in the sun’s rays, since the water of the lake itself is darker than other waters and has the appearance of being scorched. Certainly, if it too shines in a ray of sunlight, there is nothing new or to be put forward as a marvel, since this is common to all waters. It is certain that lumps of bitumen, a black liquid, drift over the water; those whose task this is approach in boats and collect them. Bitumen is said to cling together so firmly that it cannot be cut by iron or any other sharply pointed metal implement. Yet it yields to women’s blood, by the discharge of which during menstruation they are said to gain relief. It is reported to be broken apart by contact with this blood or with urine, as those who have had experience of testing it assert. It is said to be useful for joining ships’ timbers and wholesome for human bodies when mixed with medicines. The lake’s length extends five hundred and eighty stades as far as Zoaros in Arabia, its breadth a hundred and fifty stades as far as the neighbourhood of the people of Sodom, who once inhabited a very fertile region, abounding in fruits and distinguished by splendid cities. Now, however, those places are deserted and burnt out by fire. For although God had bestowed everything upon them as his gift—fields bearing abundant crops and countryside planted with vines and other fruit-bearing trees—they were ungrateful and did not keep before their eyes the power of God most high, as though he did not discern all things and behold every outrage, and as though anything could be hidden from him or escape his notice. Thus they began to confound and pollute everything with the shameful acts of their intemperance, by which they drew upon themselves divine displeasure. As the price of their crimes, fire descended from heaven to burn that region. Five cities were thus consumed, a certain shadow and semblance of which is visible in the ashes. The lands burned; the waters burn, and in them the remnants of heavenly fire are recognised. There still remain fruit green to the eye and a formed cluster of grapes, such as to arouse in onlookers the desire to eat. If you pluck them, they crumble and dissolve into ash and give off smoke as though still burning. These things learnt about the territory of Sodom ought not to have been veiled in silence, because of the punishments of the impious. For after surveying them, there can be no doubt that there will be a reward for the pious.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.19.1] Vespasian therefore filled all the strongholds or city fortifications nearest Jerusalem with detachments of the Roman army or allied forces, so that they might recognise as hostile to them all the places which they had previously thought would join them in making war against the Romans. He also sent Lucius Annius to Gerasa and captured the city by stratagem. He killed a thousand young men too, who, taken by surprise, had been deprived of escape. Very many captives were carried off, and everyone’s property was seized by the soldiers at their commander’s order. The estates they found were burned, and they exercised their licence to plunder. They ravaged everything in the mountains and on the plains, and the city of Jerusalem, surrounded by these places, blazed with war on every side. Nor were the people of Jerusalem free from awareness of their dangers: all exits had been blocked against them, so that no one might escape danger by flight. Within was the domestic evil; outside, everything was closed. There was neither the wish to remain nor the means to flee. Even anyone who had hoped for pardon from the Romans by deserting was prevented by his own people from leaving.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.20.1] Vespasian had returned to the city of Caesarea, so that, having gathered all his forces there, he might undertake the siege of Jerusalem. News arrived that Nero had been killed after completing the thirteenth year of his reign, when he was already passing the eighth day of the following year. He deserved that punishment, for he had violated not only faith by sacrilege, family devotion by the murder of kin, and chastity by incest, but also the very power of the Roman dominion, whose offices and affairs he had entrusted to the most wicked of freedmen. For since he himself kept faith with no one, he suspected everyone, and therefore thought he should entrust himself above all to the utterly wicked Nymphidius and Gemellinus, whose lowly condition had made them dependent. But even they eventually shuddered at the example of his cruelty; and because he had killed all those dearest to him, they thought they must take precautions for themselves and wished to forestall what they feared. Thus, conspiring with the others, they deserted the murderer of his kin. For whom was he thought likely to spare, when he had not spared his mother? Abandoned therefore by all his people, he fled the city with four of his freedmen. Seeing himself hard pressed by the conspirators drawing near and by a hostile force, he secretly withdrew to an estate outside the city, torn and lacerated by thorns while he feared being seen by anyone, lest he be betrayed. Then, realising that he was surrounded, he prepared a contrivance of wood and put it together with his own hands to kill himself, so that severe punishments might not be exacted from him. Turning to his freedmen, he said: “What an artist is dying!” Thus the most cruel murderer of his kin met an end to his life worthy of his deserts: he who had killed his mother and his own people did not spare even himself. Truly he was a fine artist of his own death, who devised a way of perishing such that not even his death was free from crime.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.21.1] Thus the report that Nero had been killed had arrived first, in keeping with the human disposition, which is content, on hearing what it desires, to inquire no further, but at once to spread abroad and send out among the people, still incomplete, what has pleased it. Not long afterwards, however, it became known that Galba was at the head of the Roman dominion. Vespasian therefore decided to ascertain the new emperor’s judgement on the Jewish war, and sent his son Titus and King Agrippa. Titus returned from Achaea on learning that Galba too, on the seventh day of the seventh month after taking power, had been stripped of his insignia and suffered punishment in the very heart of the city, that is, the Roman Forum, and that Otho enjoyed success and the imperial succession. Agrippa hastened to Rome to establish his favour with the new emperor. To Titus, the reverence owed to his father in family devotion seemed of greater worth than that owed to imperial power, since he thought that, if he went on without consulting his father, he would not please even the emperor himself. Certainly the outcome showed that he had returned to his father at an opportune time, amid new events whose direction was uncertain. Indeed, Vespasian too, anxious about the condition of the whole Roman dominion and his fatherland, suspended the war and restrained his own onslaught, setting what was happening in Judaea below his care for the whole state and his devoted concern for his fatherland.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.22.1] But Judaea was not at rest: it was waging a more grievous war among its own people than against outsiders. For while John’s faction was intolerable, Simon also rose up. He was inferior in wickedness of character, but relied more on his bodily frame to dare every impious deed, and was accustomed through brigandage to practising and attempting outrages. He was a citizen of Gerasa, vigorous in youth, whom Ananus, the chief priest, had brought low for his wicked schemes and driven from the place where he lived, compelling him to withdraw to other regions. But he, who had no place among the quiet and moderate, joined the company of brigands. At first they too suspected him, lest he ensnare them by intrigue; afterwards he easily insinuated himself among them through their common character. With them he ravaged the places adjoining their strongholds, because they did not dare to seek more distant places. Hiding as though in burrows, they lay in wait for passers-by without making any expedition, content, as it were, with brigandage at home. Simon, unrestrained in spirit, could not endure this for long, and soon gathered a large force for himself, promising freedom to slaves, rewards to the free, and recompense to the reprobate.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.22.3] He was already advancing surrounded by twenty thousand armed men when the people of Jerusalem suddenly grew afraid of his daily progress. Thinking that, if it continued to grow for longer, it would turn against them, they decided it must be cut short, and in a sudden armed sortie attacked Simon. He did not lie open to their ambush heedless and unprepared, but met them as they approached, routed many, and compelled others, driven from the battle, to withdraw into the city.

Thinking that, if it continued to grow for longer, it would turn against them, they decided it must be cut short, and in a sudden armed sortie attacked Simon. He did not lie open to their ambush heedless and unprepared, but met them as they approached, routed many, and compelled others, driven from the battle, to withdraw into the city.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.23.1] He also fought the Idumaeans and withdrew on equal terms, yet was distressed as though defeated because he had not won. When they were to fight again, he thought it more advantageous to try deceit and found a willing servant of fraud. For when it was understood what he sought, Jacob, one of the leaders of the Idumaeans, cunning and crafty in such affairs, came secretly to Simon and offered to betray his fatherland, giving assurance that he would ensnare all the Idumaeans. Having demanded, as the reward of their future association, that he should be the most powerful and trusted man with him, he promised to betray them all. Their friendship was sealed by a banquet, and Simon’s immense promises confirmed the agreement between them. On returning to his own people, Jacob began by telling a few that he had gone out to reconnoitre the enemy’s strength and had seen a powerful force, men experienced in war, a very great multitude invincible in battle. Gradually he introduced such talk among the leaders, and finally spread it among them all: Simon himself was exceedingly energetic; he had organised his army in the manner of a king, maintained its ranks, distributed its units and appointed capable commanders. The Idumaeans ought to look to their own interests, so as to experience such a man as a friend rather than an enemy. Certainly, if they saw him superior in an encounter, they should yield without danger and avoid battle. When Jacob learnt that the inclinations of very many had bent to his view, he instructed Simon to take the field. Confident that the Idumaeans would scatter, Simon did not delay. paragraphs.rawText: [IV.23.2] Having gained a triumph over so great a nation, he became more insolent towards the rest. He captured sooner than expected Hebron, an ancient city, thronged with people and rich in wealth, found much plunder in it and carried off its abundant produce. For it is said to be the most ancient city, not only among the cities of Palestine but also among all those founded by the ancients in Egypt, so that many think even Memphis, which is considered the most ancient, later than it. There were also those who said that father Abraham had lived in it after setting out from Mesopotamia and making for Egypt, and that his sons had a tomb there, most beautifully built of marble and of exquisite workmanship. Seven stades from the city, a great terebinth tree is asserted to have stood there since the foundation of the world; whether it still remains now, however, is unknown to us. Advancing from there, he ravaged territories, stormed cities and gathered peoples. Surrounded by forty thousand armed men, he emptied everything wherever he went, even as though a friend and ally. For what place could supply food for so many? By the mere tread of the foot soldiers, every place in which he stationed such numbers of fighting men was trampled like pavement. Not only was every crop carried away, as though eaten by locusts, but the ground, beaten into pavement, refused to bear fruit even in the future.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.23.3] The growth of Simon’s power terrified John, and all the associates of his faction were shaken. They wanted Simon destroyed but did not dare to provoke him to war. Again they prepared an ambush and, lying in wait along the roads, seized his wife with her entire female retinue and a few men escorting her. They boasted as though they had achieved a complete victory and, as though holding Simon himself captive, thought that he would supplicate them. But he was harsh and merciless, could be reached by affection for no one, and held nothing dear or sacred. He was inflamed as though by an affront received rather than a love taken away, and tortured those he found with far greater savagery and grievous torments. He cut off the hands of very many and sent them, their bodies mutilated, to the enemy, to announce his cruelty and make known his threat to overthrow the walls and destroy the city unless his own wife was restored to him at once. He would likewise mutilate the hands and entrails of all who dwelt within the city unless they took thought in time. Thus, terrified, they sent his wife to him. His fury was thereby softened, and he gave those shut in some opportunity for rest, ceasing to press the siege.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.24.1] Not only had Galba been killed, but Otho too had perished in conflict with the commanders of Vitellius, whom the army in Gaul had made emperor. In the first encounter Otho appeared the stronger. When battle was renewed a day later, Otho learnt that victory had fallen to Valens and Caecina, the companions of Vitellius, and that very many of his own men had been killed. At Brixia he rescued himself from humiliation by a voluntary death, after holding power for only three months and two days. Victorious, then, Vitellius hastened to Rome with the army that had survived on both sides.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.25.1] At that time Vespasian set out from the city of Caesarea. He ravaged Judaea and subdued all the neighbouring mountains and strongholds. He killed those who resisted, granted those who begged for mercy a pardon that spared their lives, drove his adversaries to flight and stationed his own men in their places. Cerealis too, a commander of the Roman army, ranged everywhere with the cavalry, destroying some, subduing others and driving along columns of captives. Everything around Jerusalem was burned, so that the Jews might have no refuge. Thus every way out had been blocked against the Jews before the siege.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.25.2] But they not only failed to look to their own interests; they also fought out a domestic contest among themselves. John was the tyrant within, Simon the enemy outside the walls. After receiving his wife back, Simon went on a brief expedition, ravaged Idumaea, and returned stronger, making his arms resound around the walls of Jerusalem. John, stationed within, trained his men for war through vice, giving them licence for crimes. Zeal for plunder, desires for shameful acts, outpourings of luxury and the scents of ointments seethed. They curled their hair with curling irons, painted their eyes with antimony and put on women’s clothing. They sought not only women’s adornment but also feminine softness and the passions of unlawful lusts. Men practised women’s ways, made their voices effeminate and undid their sex by the languor of their bodies; they grew their hair, whitened their faces, smoothed their cheeks with pumice, plucked their beards, and in this dissolution practised an intolerable savagery of cruelty. Indeed, they walked with a mincing gait, yet in a moment became warriors: suddenly drawing the swords they kept concealed beneath their purple cloaks, they slashed apart whoever they found. Whoever had escaped Simon was killed by John if he withdrew within the city; whoever had fled John was captured by Simon and sacrificed before the walls.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.25.3] The dissension was grievous. The Idumaeans sought to extinguish John’s tyranny: they envied his power and hated his cruelty. They fought against the attendants of the tyranny, drove them back and pursued them as far as the royal palace, which a close female relative of the king of Adiabene had founded. They rushed in, drove out its defenders, occupied the temple and plundered the spoils of the tyranny, since John had established a storehouse for his wealth there. A grave fear arose that the Idumaeans would enter the city from the temple by night, kill the populace with the sword and destroy the city by fire. Terrified by this fear, after deliberation they brought in another tyrant, since they could not endure the one. John had crept into tyranny by fraud; this man, invited as though he would provide a remedy for their safety, brought domination upon the citizens and a tyrant upon the city. Matthias, the chief priest, was sent to beg him to enter. With great arrogance he consented to rule, and, as though it were a burden, yielded to their entreaties and poured into the city with his whole force. They opened the gates with their own hands to admit a more destructive man, while cursing the one within. Thus Simon, having entered as he wished, showed himself equally an enemy to all. With a common hatred of everyone he persecuted both those who had called him in and those against whom his help had been sought. John was hard pressed by his own deceits; the city tossed upon the waves. The contest between John and Simon was who could do more harm to his own people.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.26.1] Reports of civil wars gained strength in the Roman army. The deaths of Galba and Otho became known, and the rule of Vitellius, who, more wicked than his predecessors, had settled like dregs. Veteran soldiers began to confer among themselves and resent the presumption of the praetorian legions at Rome: although they had long ceased to experience the dangers of war and did not know the names of the nations that made war, they nevertheless appointed an emperor for wars and claimed that the choice of the arbiter of Roman affairs lay in their hands. Then, following this example, the soldiers stationed in Gaul had aspired to give Vitellius imperial power without consulting the senate and Roman people. They themselves meanwhile were treated as mercenaries, following the decisions of others, first in danger and last in honour. For so long they had waged war, with their triumphs increasing daily, yet received masters from their inferiors—not even useful ones, but men utterly idle or devoted to their bellies and to disgrace. They must confront and remove this injury. They had an energetic man in Vespasian, whom everyone ought to have chosen as emperor, mature in years for counsel and stronger than younger men in battle. They must hasten, lest others choose him first, to the discredit of those with whom he had grown old in military service and triumphs. When was there a more opportune time to repay his labours with a worthy reward? Vitellius’s voracity was a disgrace to private citizens, to say nothing of emperors. Neither the senate nor the Roman people would endure for long that this disgrace of drunkards should remain at the summit of imperial power, a man for whose expenditure the Roman state could not suffice. “For who could endure a tyrant’s rule when he has in the army a worthy governor of the Roman dominion? What nations would subject themselves to luxury and surrender to vice, when an emperor’s idleness is an incentive to war, whereas the firmness of peace rests on valour in an enemy and sobriety in the ruler of the state? Who would not admire in Vespasian, still a private citizen, the splendour of kingship and the authority of the Roman dominion, when so many military units and the stronger force of the whole Roman army are at his disposal? Why do we wait, so that, supported by our valour, he may owe to others his position as emperor, and we may yield to others what lies within our rightful power? Certainly, if we do not wish to honour him, let us not disparage him or inflict this injury: that by our judgement he should be rejected as unworthy of the imperial power of which Vitellius is held worthy. Finally, since his brother and his son Domitian are in Italy, there is surely reason to fear that a man who should long ago have been a distinction to his family may become a danger to them. Or, if they begin, as we suppose, to press the tyrant, their rebellion as his brother and son may count against him, and we may begin to see as an accused man the one whom we are unwilling to see as emperor.”

At last they surrounded him under arms as he struggled against them, threatening death with their swords. They recognised that guilt and grave danger would remain with them if he refused. Thus he yielded to their pressure rather than willingly accepting what others commonly solicit. The soldiers pressed him, the commanders urged him; he took on the burden before the honour.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.26.3] He hastened to Egypt, for he knew that the greatest resources of the Roman state were there. Where its sustenance was supplied, he must seek support for himself if he won, or a means of obstructing Vitellius if he thought the war should be prolonged. There were also two military formations there, which he hastened to join to himself, so that a very great city, surrounded by numerous natural defences and highly useful for either outcome of the war, might remain under his own authority rather than another’s. We have therefore thought that something should be said, even briefly, about the situation of the places, and above all about the chief city itself.
