paragraphs.rawText: [IV.27.1] The city of Alexandria was founded by Alexander, to whom the name of a great commander was given for his valour. It lies like a barrier between Egypt and the sea, a city with poor harbourage, like most of Egypt, and difficult of access from outside, situated in the more remote parts of Asia. To the west Egypt itself borders on the arid regions of Libya; its southern and upper regions separate Syene and the unnavigable cataracts of the river Nile from the Ethiopians. On the east the Red Sea spreads back as far as Coptos, a place at the furthest edge of the land which opens a passage to the Indians for those about to sail. Enclosed therefore on one side by the burning heat of the sun, on that side by the Indian sea and on this by the Egyptian sea, it adjoins land only along a single northern wall leading into Syria. The rest is shut off on every side and fortified by the aid of nature. Yet the protection of its northern side is divided and opens through a kind of double threshold, through which either foreign supplies are conveyed to it over the Egyptian sea or freer access extends overland. The land stretches to an immeasurable extent. For between Syene and Pelusium lies an immense length of two thousand stades, if the statements are to be believed, and from Plinthine to Pelusium likewise three thousand six hundred stades. The region is unaccustomed to rains, yet has no need of them, since the Nile’s irrigation supplies showers of its own accord. The Nile is both things to it: the abundance of heaven and the fertility of earth. It tempers the fields and enriches the soil, equally useful to sailors and farmers. The former sail, the latter sow; these are carried about their own fields in boats, those cultivate them: sowing without a plough, travelling without a carriage. You may see the land divided by streams and raised, as it were, by ramparts of ships. Dwellings wander across all the lands encircled by the Nile. For it is navigable as far as the city they call the City of Elephants. Beyond it the cataracts we have mentioned do not allow a ship to proceed, not through lack of depth but through the whole river’s steep descent and a kind of collapse of the waters. The city’s harbour, like most approaches along the coast, is difficult to enter, and far more difficult than the others. It resembles the form of a human body: more capacious in the head itself and the anchorage, narrower in the throat, where it receives the passage of the sea and ships, which supply the harbour with a kind of aid to breathing. When one has passed the narrows and mouth of the harbour, the expanse of the sea stretches far and wide like the rest of the body. On the right of the harbour is a small island, and on it a very great tower, which Greeks and Latins alike have called Pharos from its very function: it is seen from afar by sailors, so that, before they approach the harbour, especially at night, the indication of its flames lets them know that land is near. Thus they will not be deceived by darkness and strike the rocks or fail to find the bounds of the entrance. There are attendants there who kindle the fire by placing torches and other piles of wood beneath it. Like a herald of the land and a guide to the harbour’s throat, it shows the narrow approach, the recesses of the waves and the windings of the entrance, lest a frail keel graze the crags and strike rocks hidden beneath the waves at the very entrance. The straight course must therefore be turned aside a little, lest the ship strike unseen rocks and incur danger where escape from dangers is hoped for. For the approach to the harbour is narrower, constricted on the right by the island’s flank and on the left by rocks which obstruct the harbour’s left side. Around the island too, built masses of enormous size are lowered into place, lest the island’s foundations yield to the constant onslaught of the rising sea and be loosened by long-standing damage. Hence, as the waves strike the side of the island and recoil in the opposite direction among the jagged rocks and constructed masses, the channel between is always restless, and the roughened passage makes entry dangerous for ships. The extent of the harbour is thirty stades, its anchorage safe and its calm very great in any storm. For by the narrows of the aforesaid mouth and the barrier of the island it repels the waves of the sea. The harbour within is made utterly safe as a kind of compensation for the dangerous entrance: by those same narrows of the harbour mouth, the whole basin is defended, kept free from storms and calmed from the crashing waves that make the entrance rough. Nor is it without reason that the protection and size of the harbour are such, since things serving the needs of the whole world must be conveyed into it. For the innumerable peoples of those places seek the trade of the whole world for their own use; and the region, fruitful in crops and abounding in the other gifts of the earth and in commerce, feeds the whole world with grain and supplies it with necessary goods.

Thus they will not be deceived by darkness and strike the rocks or fail to find the bounds of the entrance. There are attendants there who kindle the fire by placing torches and other piles of wood beneath it. Like a herald of the land and a guide to the harbour’s throat, it shows the narrow approach, the recesses of the waves and the windings of the entrance, lest a frail keel graze the crags and strike rocks hidden beneath the waves at the very entrance. The straight course must therefore be turned aside a little, lest the ship strike unseen rocks and incur danger where escape from dangers is hoped for. For the approach to the harbour is narrower, constricted on the right by the island’s flank and on the left by rocks which obstruct the harbour’s left side. Around the island too, built masses of enormous size are lowered into place, lest the island’s foundations yield to the constant onslaught of the rising sea and be loosened by long-standing damage. Hence, as the waves strike the side of the island and recoil in the opposite direction among the jagged rocks and constructed masses, the channel between is always restless, and the roughened passage makes entry dangerous for ships. The extent of the harbour is thirty stades, its anchorage safe and its calm very great in any storm. For by the narrows of the aforesaid mouth and the barrier of the island it repels the waves of the sea. The harbour within is made utterly safe as a kind of compensation for the dangerous entrance: by those same narrows of the harbour mouth, the whole basin is defended, kept free from storms and calmed from the crashing waves that make the entrance rough. Nor is it without reason that the protection and size of the harbour are such, since things serving the needs of the whole world must be conveyed into it. For the innumerable peoples of those places seek the trade of the whole world for their own use; and the region, fruitful in crops and abounding in the other gifts of the earth and in commerce, feeds the whole world with grain and supplies it with necessary goods.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.28.1] Having therefore settled affairs in Alexandria in his favour, with the support of all who conducted military affairs united around his rule, he felt secure in his absence and hastened his return to Syria. He had, however, approached Tiberius Alexander, who then governed Egypt, with instructions to attach to him the goodwill of the army in the upper regions, and himself to help bear, with whatever forces he could, the burden of Roman rule that had been laid upon Vespasian. Tiberius made the letter known to the provincials and soldiers. It was received by all with joy; allegiance was promised and favour poured forth. Caesarea received Vespasian, then Berytus, with embassies from the cities flocking to him in the greatest joy.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.28.2] There Josephus too was ordered to be released from his bonds. Titus approached the emperor to ask that the chains be broken rather than loosened, because, if they were broken, it would be as though he had not been bound. This pleased his father. He ordered an axe to be brought and the chains to be broken, so that the Jews might realise that pardon would not be denied to them either, if they changed their course and asked for peace. At the same time, he did so because he was no longer keeping Josephus for another’s judgement, since authority to decide all matters had now been conferred upon himself.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.29.1] They came to Antioch. There, after deliberation on where they ought to cross to Italy, speed was the consideration, since he had seen that everything in Egypt and Alexandria was secure. He therefore sent Mucianus ahead with a large part of the cavalry and infantry, to precede the emperor’s arrival in Italy. Deterred by fear of a long voyage, Mucianus directed his route through Cappadocia and Phrygia.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.29.2] He also ordered Antonius, commander of the third military formation stationed in Moesia, to pour into Italy while it was unprepared, before the Vitellians stirred. For Vitellius, as though surfeited and sunk in sleep, thought he was managing a banquet rather than an empire, and slumbered amid affairs of such importance. Indeed, scarcely roused at last by news of Antonius’s approach, he sent Caecina with part of the army and entrusted the whole issue of his danger to another’s judgement, relying on Caecina’s strength because he had routed Otho’s force. Caecina met Antonius as he approached near the city of Cremona, reconnoitred everything and learnt that a very powerful force was coming against him, energetic in war and practised in triumphs. His own men, by contrast, were equal neither in strength nor in number and could not fight against the stronger force. He summoned the centurions and urged them to desist from war, since they were inferior in number and the other emperor’s glory carried greater weight. The fame of the commander conducting the whole undertaking counted for much in war. Vespasian had shone in the regions of Gaul and in victories in Britain; Vespasian, girded with triumphs in the East, rested on a strong presumption in favour of his name. Vitellius, nothing but a man dissolved in wine and always belching yesterday’s feasts amid his banquets, expected nothing except to perish drunk, without feeling pain, when the enemy arrived. The glory of so great an emperor raised the spirits of the soldiers on the one side; on the other, his disgrace and shameful acts cast them down. They must take care not to lose the fame of the former war. They had defeated Otho, Vitellius’s equal; now they had to deal with a man who had encircled the whole world with his triumphs. They must forestall necessity by goodwill, choosing Vespasian as a fellow citizen rather than experiencing him as an enemy. It was wretched even to win in a civil war. “How much more wretched to be defeated, so that you appear an enemy of your own people! The victor retains his fatherland; the defeated man loses it, or, if it remains, it will remain to the odium of his crime, so that we appear to have made war upon our fellow citizens for a tyrant. For the defeated man is no longer a citizen but a tyrant. Why do we join guilty hands in battle? Let it be enough for our guilt to have won once, so that we were ashamed of the man for whom we won. We thought he would become sober at least through imperial power, or, awakened by the weight of affairs, renounce his perpetual sleep. Why do we wait any longer? Our dangers win no gratitude from any of our fellow soldiers; our judgements are reproved and condemned by all peoples because of the outrages of the man we chose. Consider what kind of man he is, rejected even as a victor. We must certainly deliberate first on the outcome of the war, and then fight. If dangers come first, you will deliberate in vain; once a plan has been approved, you may rightly begin.” He added that, as befitted a vigilant commander, he had reconnoitred everything, and it had become clear that Vespasian’s army was stronger. His allegiance to Vitellius had long since been proved. When he had been confident of the outcome of war, victory had followed; when he lacked confidence, what would happen was plain. He did not fear his own death, but the danger to the Roman army and, what pains men more, the loss of glory already won, so that those accustomed to victory should appear defeated. He must certainly take care lest it be judged that his victory in the former war had been due not to courage but to chance, and his later defeat to cowardice.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.30.1] By these and similar words he brought the soldiers over to his view, so that they would go with him to Antonius and surrender themselves to him voluntarily. But such is the changeability of the crowd, especially a military one: during the night, in their beds, many were stung by remorse for having deserted Vitellius, lest, if he proved the stronger, no room for pardon should remain for those who had abandoned their own emperor. They rose and began to confer, first with whoever they encountered and then with everyone, on how to amend their error. Drawing their swords, they sprang upon Caecina, wishing to avenge the injury of their own lapse. But when the centurions and chiliarchs intervened, they thought they should indeed refrain from killing him, yet prepared to send him bound to Vitellius. Learning this, Antonius moved the men he had brought with him and rushed under arms upon the deserters. On seeing the column of the opposing side, they prepared for battle. But after daring to resist for a little while, they turned to flee to Cremona. Antonius met them with his horsemen and forestalled every approach, so that the fugitives would not be received, and killed them, shut out before the city.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.30.2] A very great multitude was killed there; he pursued the rest into the city itself and destroyed them. Everything was plundered. Very many merchants who had come from other places, and very many inhabitants, were killed for the sake of plunder while defending their possessions. Thirty thousand two hundred men of Vitellius’s army who were present were destroyed. Primus too—for that was Antonius’s surname—lost four thousand five hundred of the Moesian soldiers. For when the Vitellians saw themselves surrounded, despairing of safety and wishing to avenge themselves, they too yielded no bloodless victory to Antonius’s men. Caecina was released from his bonds and sent by Antonius to Vespasian. There, not only assurance of safety but also the payment of rewards consoled him for the stain of betrayal.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.31.1] Elated by the news of this victory, Sabinus wished to win favour for himself too with the emperor by forestalling Antonius’s arrival through the destruction or expulsion of Vitellius; or, if Vitellius resisted, Antonius, who was reported to be on the very point of arriving, would come to his aid. He therefore gathered soldiers for himself, a force drawn from the units stationed at Rome to perform watch duties.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.31.2] At night he also occupied the Capitol. During the day very many nobles flocked to him, among them Domitian, born to Vespasian’s brother, who feared that the vengeance of Vitellius might be turned upon him as Vespasian’s nephew. Placed between two opponents, Vitellius attacked the nearer, less concerned about the more distant—for dangers close at hand inspire greater fear. In his indignation he sent the Germans against the Capitol. Exceedingly fierce in the savagery of their nation, and also stronger in number, they surrounded Sabinus’s fighting band.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.31.3] Almost all were killed. Domitian, however, with many of the nobles, found an opportunity to flee while the Germans strove to reach the upper parts of the Capitol and were repelled by Sabinus and his companions with the aid of their position. Or perhaps he himself too was being preserved for the public evil, as a future tyrant. Vitellius tortured Sabinus and killed him; all the gifts offered to the Capitol were plundered and the temple was burned.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.32.1] A day later Antonius arrived and met them from the opposite side. After three encounters around the city’s walls, all the Vitellians were routed and killed. Meanwhile Vitellius was feasting, lest, about to die, he miss his meal; as men commonly do in their last moments, he stuffed himself with the more abundant dishes of his final table. He overwhelmed himself with more frequent cups of wine, so as to lose awareness of the disgrace or danger to come. He was snatched from the banquet and dragged through the crowd; insults were hurled at the dying man, and injuries inflicted which, drunk, he did not feel. He was killed in the middle of the city, pouring out wine and blood together and belching his drunken excess. Had he lived longer, he would have licked away the wealth of the Roman dominion in expenditure on luxury and the cost of his tables. Indeed, he ruled for eight months and five days, and already Rome had failed to satisfy his appetite. More than fifty thousand others were counted among the slain.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.33.1] On the following day Mucianus and Antonius entered together with the army and scarcely put an end to the killing by the raging soldiers. For they pursued the Vitellians as men who had presumed to determine who should rule, and searched the houses of private citizens, stirred by such indignation that, when they discovered some of the people hiding in fear, they struck them as Vitellians before an inquiry could reveal the truth. Thus the victors’ fury often forestalled questioning. Since Vespasian was absent, Mucianus put Domitian in charge of public affairs, as though to fill an interregnum, lest prosperity lack any blemish. Yet the lust for outrages had not wholly poured itself into Domitian. He was still unpractised in vices and a novice in crimes as in positions of power.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.33.2] Vespasian, detained by winter, with the sea closed by winds, returned to Alexandria with his son. There, on receiving news of victory and learning of the Roman populace’s favour towards him, he decided to hasten his departure, lest anything new be attempted in his absence. Yet he did not leave the Jewish war unattended. He thought it should be entrusted to his son as a partner in his works and his successor, so that neither the Romans should lack him in person nor the Jews lack Vespasian, whom his son would represent.

paragraphs.rawText: [IV.33.3] Chosen therefore to carry out his father’s triumph, Titus was sent with a picked force. He set out on foot and made for Nicopolis. That city is twenty-four stades from Alexandria. From there, putting his soldiers aboard a fleet of larger ships, he sailed down the Nile as far as the city of Thmuis. Advancing from there, he stayed in the city called Tanis. The travellers’ second stopping-place was the city of Heraclea, the third Pelusium. After spending two days at Pelusium as a halt, he travelled through the desert and reached the temple of Jupiter Casius. Ostracine was his next stopping-place. It lacked local water, yet by their diligence the inhabitants had provided themselves with a supply by constructing water conduits. The Rhinocori too received the advancing army with welcome refreshment. They came to the city of Raphiul, which marks the beginning of Syria for those travelling from Egypt. They reached Gaza—this was the fifth city for those arriving—then Ascalon, then Jamnia, from which they passed to Joppa and reached Caesarea. There it was necessary to remain for a little while and gather the force of soldiers still in winter quarters. Already the rigour of winter was abating.
